We use the phrases [backend](https://github.com/search?q=repo%3AOWASP%2FASVS+%22backend%22+path%3A%2F%5E5%5C.0%5C%2Fen%5C%2F%2F&type=code) and [back-end](https://github.com/search?q=repo%3AOWASP%2FASVS+%22back-end%22+path%3A%2F%5E5.0%5C%2Fen%5C%2F%2F&type=code) interchangeably.

We need to decide which to use and use it consistently.

comments.body:
* front-end vs frontend
* pre-whatever vs prewhatever

I was looking for usage and definitions and found this funny case: the relevant [AWS page](https://aws.amazon.com/compare/the-difference-between-frontend-and-backend/) uses "Frontend" in the page text, but "Front End" in the title (`document.title`). Madness!

Personally, I have never loved these terms because they have had inconsistent usage, but it probably makes sense to align with Amazon's use (on the page, not the title). Initial suggestion:

- **Frontend** - The client-side (user-facing) functionality of an application, such as the user interface. 
- **Backend** - The server-side functionality of an application, including APIs and processing of HTTP requests.

"client" may be ambiguous. In server-to-server communications, many clients are not frontend.

Suggestion:

> Frontend - The user-facing functionality of an application, such as the user interface, typically executed on user-controlled device or another local device. In the context of ASVS, this is typically executed in the user's browser (HTML, JavaScript, etc.) <del>but may include other user-side applications (such as a native authorization application)</del>.
>
> Backend - The server-side functionality of an application, including APIs and processing of HTTP requests.
Although those are related, I think the issue is about the style, not about the meaning or definition.

These terms really matter a lot. Like @randomstuff was saying above, the notion of "client" is contextual:

- When thinking about frontend-backend interactions, a client is typically user-facing software.
- In backend systems, a client is often another server interacting with dependent services.

This  gets really confusing especially with older developers who came from the API monolith world.

@elarlang I know the intent of the issue was for consistency/style, but IMO it's the right opportunity to settle on definitions to ensure the terms are - in fact - used consistently. To that end, I second @randomstuff's proposal.

You seem to have some theoretical exercise here over the terms. To have more precise focus and defined "problem to solve", I provide the usage of front-?end and back-? end.

## The usage of "backend"

Requirements:
* V2.6.2 Verify that, when being stored in the application's back-end, lookup secrets with less than 112 bits of entropy (19 random alphanumeric characters or 34 random digits) are hashed with an approved password storage hashing algorithm that incorporates a 32-bit random salt. A standard hash function can be used if the secret has 112 bits of entropy or more.
* V3.1.2 Verify that the application performs all session token verification using a trusted, back-end service.
* V7.2.6 Verify that the application logs security control failures such as backend TLS failures.
* V13.6.2 Verify that HTTP requests using the HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE or GET verb do not modify any backend data structure or perform any state-changing actions. These requests are safe methods and should therefore not have any side effects.
* V14.6.2 Verify that communications between back-end application components, including local or operating system services, APIs, middleware and data layers, are performed with accounts assigned the least necessary privileges.
* V14.7.1 Verify that communications between back-end application components which don't support the application's standard user session mechanism, including APIs, middleware and data layers, are authenticated. Authentication should use individual service accounts, short-term tokens or certificate based authentication and not unchanging credentials such as passwords, API keys or shared accounts with privileged access.
* V14.8.1 Verify that a secrets management solution such as a key vault is used to securely create, store, control access to, and destroy back-end secrets. These could include passwords, key material, integrations with databases and third-party systems, seeds and internal secrets, and API keys. Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts. For a L3 application, this should involve a hardware-backed solution such as an HSM.
* V14.8.2 Verify that key material is not exposed to the application (neither the front-end nor the back-end) but instead uses an isolated security module like a vault for cryptographic operations.
* V51.1.1 Verify that tokens are only sent to components that strictly need them. For example, avoid having access or refresh tokens accessible for the frontend when they are only needed by the backend.
* V51.4.15 Verify that, for a server-side client (which is not executed on the end-user device), the authorization server ensures that the 'authorization_details' parameter value is from the client backend and that the user has not tampered with it. For example by requiring the usage of pushed authorization request (PAR) or JWT-secured authorization request (JAR).


## The usage of "frontend"

* Chapter title: "V50 Web Frontend Security"
* Section title: "V1.50 Web Frontend Security Documentation"

Requirements:
* V14.8.2 Verify that key material is not exposed to the application (neither the front-end nor the back-end) but instead uses an isolated security module like a vault for cryptographic operations.
* V51.1.1 Verify that tokens are only sent to components that strictly need them. For example, avoid having access or refresh tokens accessible for the frontend when they are only needed by the backend.

Jim, do you validate the AI output?

> Chapter Title (V50 Web Frontend Security):

> The chapter focuses specifically on the web front-end but references both front-end and back-end concerns in its requirements (e.g., JSONP in V50.5.1 ).
> Potential confusion: This overlap might blur the boundary of what "frontend security" entails versus overall application security.

Entire chapter does not mentioned "back" at once. Requirement V50.5.1 is:
> V50.5.1 [ADDED] Verify that JSONP functionality is not enabled anywhere across the application to avoid Cross-Site Script Inclusion (XSSI) attacks.

Served like that, it is a useless noise. Please don't do that and waste the time of others who need to work it through.

> You seem to have some theoretical exercise here over the terms.

These terms are used so widely that the proper approach would be to adopt the industry consensus (to the extent it can be established) and ensure that requirements conform.

I am not convinced there is industry consensus over whether it is hyphenated, spaced or neither.

> I was looking for usage and definitions and found this funny case: the relevant [AWS page](https://aws.amazon.com/compare/the-difference-between-frontend-and-backend/) uses "Frontend" in the page text, but "Front End" in the title (`document.title`). Madness!

@ryarmst I see your AWS madness and raise you this spectacular specimen, [also from AWS documentation](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mobile/backends-for-frontends-pattern/).

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a345eeb6-ddad-46b0-a49e-768c92930ffb)

---

The Bishop Fox styleguide uses either spacing or hyphenation:
* https://bishopfox.com/cybersecurity-style-guide/list-of-terms/f#front-end
* https://bishopfox.com/cybersecurity-style-guide/list-of-terms/b#back-end

But then it also seems to [include](https://bishopfox.com/cybersecurity-style-guide/list-of-terms/b#borg) a [bunch](https://bishopfox.com/cybersecurity-style-guide/list-of-terms/f#ftl) of [Star Wars](https://bishopfox.com/cybersecurity-style-guide/list-of-terms/h#hyperdrive) and [Star Trek](https://bishopfox.com/cybersecurity-style-guide/list-of-terms/w#warp-drive) terms so I am not sure I want to reference it as a source 🤣🤣🤣

---

On a more serious note, I had a quick look [at a](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/style-guide/punctuation/dashes-hyphens/hyphens) [few](https://www.grammarly.com/blog/punctuation-capitalization/hyphen/) [sources](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/punctuation/hyphens) and I don't feel that backend and frontend really warrant hyphens because they are words which basically stand by themselves at this point. 

You could in theory make an argument that they could be used differently in different contexts but I personally believe that using them without a space or a hyphen is the cleanest option

**Edit:**

i.e. I propose that we should universally be using "backend" and "frontend"
